When you are stuck choosing between two bad options, and you pick the one that is less bad — the one that will cause less harm, less trouble, or less suffering — you are choosing "the lesser of two evils."

The key idea is this: neither option is good. Both are bad. But one is worse than the other. So you reluctantly choose the one that hurts less.

Simple breakdown of the phrase:

  • Lesser = smaller, not as great, not as bad
  • Evil = something bad, harmful, or unpleasant
  • Two evils = two bad choices

So "the lesser of two evils" = the less harmful of two bad choices.
A Simple Everyday Example

Imagine you hate both going to the dentist and having a toothache. You have two choices:

  1. Live with the toothache (painful, gets worse over time)
  2. Go to the dentist (scary and uncomfortable, but fixes the problem)

You choose to go to the dentist. It's still unpleasant — but it's less bad than letting the toothache destroy your tooth. You have chosen the lesser of two evils.
The Core Feeling Behind This Idiom

This idiom captures a very specific human feeling: reluctant acceptance.

You are not happy about your choice. You didn't want either option. But since you must choose, you go with the one that damages you least. There is often a sense of resignation — a quiet "I don't like this, but it's the best I can do given the situation."

This is why people often say it with a sigh, or as a way of explaining why they made a choice they aren't proud of:

"I didn't want to take that job, but it paid better than the other one. It was the lesser of two evils."
How It Is Used in a Sentence

The idiom is usually used in one of these patterns:

Pattern 1: Choosing between two things

"Both candidates were disappointing, so I voted for the lesser of two evils."

Pattern 2: Explaining a past decision

"I took the highway even though there was a toll. The backroads would've taken an hour longer — it was the lesser of two evils."

Pattern 3: As a general philosophy or statement

"Sometimes in life, you don't get a perfect option. You just have to pick the lesser of two evils."

Pattern 4: With "choose" or "pick"

"When you can't win either way, you just pick the lesser of two evils and move on."
Important Nuance: It Must Be Exactly Two Options

This idiom is specifically about two bad choices, not three or four. The word "two" in the phrase is deliberate. When you say it, you're signaling:

  • I had exactly two paths in front of me.
  • Both were bad.
  • I picked the less damaging one.

If there were three bad options, you would not normally use this phrase — you'd say something like "the least bad option" or "the best of a bad situation."
Why "Evil"? It Sounds Dramatic

You might wonder: why use the word evil? Does it mean something truly wicked?

Not necessarily. In this idiom, "evil" is used in a broad, old-fashioned sense meaning anything harmful, unpleasant, or bad — not just morally wicked things. It's a formal or literary use of the word.

So "evil" here can refer to:

  • A painful experience (surgery vs. chronic pain)
  • An unpleasant duty (paying a fine vs. going to court)
  • A moral dilemma (a difficult political vote)
  • A personal sacrifice (a job you dislike vs. unemployment)

The word "evil" gives the phrase a slightly dramatic, philosophical weight — it hints that the choice is a serious one with real consequences.
Real-Life Situations Where This Idiom Applies

This idiom comes up everywhere — in politics, medicine, business, personal life:

Politics:
Voters often feel they have to choose between two imperfect candidates. Neither one fully represents their values, but they vote for the one they find least objectionable. People frequently describe this as "voting for the lesser of two evils."

Medicine:
A doctor might recommend a treatment that has difficult side effects. The patient doesn't want those side effects, but the alternative — leaving the illness untreated — is far worse. The treatment is the lesser of two evils.

Work:
You might have to choose between staying late at the office or missing a deadline. Neither is ideal, but you stay late because that's the lesser of two evils.

Personal decisions:
Telling a friend a hard truth might hurt them. But letting them continue making a mistake would hurt them more. The difficult truth is the lesser of two evils.
The Deeper Philosophical Idea

This phrase isn't just an idiom — it reflects a real concept in philosophy and ethics called the problem of moral dilemmas: situations where every available choice comes at a cost.

The ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle discussed choosing the lesser harm as a form of practical wisdom. The Latin phrase "e malis minimum" (meaning "choose the least of evils") expresses the same idea and is thousands of years old. The idiom in its modern English form has been in use since at least the 1300s, appearing in the writings of Geoffrey Chaucer.

The idea has stayed alive for so long because life genuinely presents these situations constantly — in governments, in hospitals, in families, and in personal choices. It's a timeless human experience.
What This Idiom Does NOT Mean

To be precise, here are things this idiom does not mean:

  • It does not mean you like your choice. You are still unhappy with it.
  • It does not mean the choice is good — only that it's less bad.
  • It does not apply when one option is clearly fine or neutral. Both must be genuinely bad or undesirable for the idiom to fit.
  • It is not the same as "making the best of a situation." That phrase is more optimistic — it implies finding something positive. "The lesser of two evils" has no positive spin. It's purely about minimizing damage.
Similar Expressions

These phrases carry a similar meaning and are good to know alongside this idiom:

  • "Between a rock and a hard place" — stuck between two difficult options with no easy way out.
  • "The best of a bad bunch/lot" — the least bad choice among several poor options.
  • "Damage control" — taking the action that limits how bad things get (not the same idiom, but the same spirit).
  • "Hobson's choice" — technically this means no real choice at all (take this or nothing), which is slightly different but often confused with "lesser of two evils."
Summary

What it meansChoosing the less harmful of two bad options
ToneReluctant, resigned, practical
When to use itWhen both choices are bad, but one is clearly worse
What it signals"I didn't want either option, but I went with the less damaging one"

The next time you face a situation where every road leads to some trouble, but one road leads to less trouble — and you take it — you are choosing the lesser of two evils. It's not a happy phrase, but it is an honest one. It acknowledges that life sometimes offers no perfect path, only a wiser one.
